title: The oldest complete song we have was carved on a tombstone
body: The Seikilos epitaph is a marble column found near Tralles, now Aydın in Turkey, around 1883, and kept today in the National Museum of Denmark. Carved on it, with Ancient Greek vocal notation above the words, is a short song: **as long as you’re alive, shine**, don’t be sad at all; life is short, and time asks for its due. It most likely dates from the first or second century AD and is the oldest surviving complete piece of music, notation included. Older notated music exists, such as the Hurrian hymn to Nikkal from Ugarit of about 1400 BC, but that survives only substantially complete and its reading is still debated.

slides.text: As long as you’re alive, shine, don’t be sad at all; life is short, time asks for its due.

slides.prompt: The stone’s last line, naming who the song was for, is missing. Why?
slides.answer: It was ground off so the finder’s wife could use the stone as a flowerpot stand
slides.detail: Before that, the dedication read Seikilos to Euterpe: possibly his wife, or perhaps the Muse of lyric poetry.

events.text: Found during railway building in Aydın

slides.question: Why is the Seikilos epitaph called the oldest complete song, rather than the older Hurrian hymn?
slides.explanation: The Hurrian hymn of about 1400 BC is older but only substantially complete, and how to read it is debated; the Seikilos song survives whole, words and notation.
